title: Ring-trial data
text:
Near-duplicate soils



near_dup_groups
def near_dup_groups(
    spectra, # `Spectra` of one instrument
    min_corr:float=0.9999, # Smallest correlation of SNV spectra for two soils to join a group
)->numpy.ndarray: # Group label of each soil, in the order of `spectra.sample_ids`
Group soils whose SNV spectra correlate above min_corr, directly or through other soils of the group


Some ring-trial soils are near-duplicates: their spectra are almost the same, and so are their properties. A split must keep such soils on one side, or the test set holds soils that the model has seen in training. near_dup_groups links two soils when their SNV spectra correlate above min_corr, and gives each connected set of soils one label. On the KSSL instrument, three groups have more than one soil:

groups = near_dup_groups(rt['KSSL'])
ids = rt['KSSL'].sample_ids
dups = [list(ids[groups == g]) for g in np.unique(groups) if (groups == g).sum() > 1]
test_eq(dups, [['RT_04', 'RT_05', 'RT_07', 'RT_13', 'RT_15'], ['RT_10', 'RT_19'], ['RT_24', 'RT_25']])

title: Ring-trial data
text:
Ring-trial soils in OSSL
60 of the ring-trial soils come from KSSL, the largest part of OSSL. A model pretrained on all of OSSL has seen the ring-trial soils that OSSL contains, with their properties. Its scores on those soils are too good. ossl_matches finds, for each ring-trial soil, the OSSL sample whose SNV spectrum correlates best with it. It then compares their clay, pH and exchangeable K. A missing ring-trial value counts as the same.



ossl_matches
def ossl_matches(
    rt_spectra, # `Spectra` of one ring-trial instrument
    ossl_mir, # OSSL MIR `Spectra` on the same wavenumbers, such as `load_ossl().mir(650, 4000)`
    tol:float=0.001, # Largest difference for two property values to count as the same
)->pandas.DataFrame: # One row per ring-trial soil, indexed by sample ID
The OSSL sample whose SNV spectrum correlates best with each ring-trial soil, and whether their clay, pH and K are the same


On the KSSL instrument, 38 soils have an OSSL match with the same clay, pH and K. All 38 are KSSL soils. None of the 10 NAPT soils is in OSSL. ossl_overlap lists the 38 OSSL samples, which pretraining leaves out:

ossl_mir = load_ossl().mir(650, 4000)
matches = ossl_matches(rt['KSSL'], ossl_mir)
test_eq(sorted(matches.ossl_id[matches.same_props]), ossl_overlap)
matches.groupby(rt['KSSL'].source.loc[matches.index, 'source']).same_props.sum().to_dict()

{'KSSL': 38, 'NAPT': 0}


The 38 matches correlate at 0.99999 or more. They differ by about 0.1% of the spectrum. It is not known whether they are two scans of the same soil or one scan processed twice. The best matches of the other soils correlate at up to 0.99992, for RT_10 and RT_23, but their properties differ. They stay in pretraining:

title: Ring-trial data
text:
Flagged soils
The outlier analysis of tidy-mirs flags four ring-trial soils. It measures Mahalanobis distances in a PCA of the spectra, after SNV and a Savitzky-Golay filter, and in the space of clay and organic carbon. Both cutoffs were set by eye, in a gap of the distances. Flagged means unusual, not wrong. The four soils stay in every analysis, and the error analysis of the transfer experiments tests whether any of them has a bad scan or a wet-chemistry error. rt_flagged gives the reason for each soil:
Three of them are rich in organic carbon, with 11% to 49%. RT_42, at 49%, also has the lowest pH of the ring trial:

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
WarningWork in progress



Pretraining and the zero-shot experiment have run. The other experiments below are still to come.
This project tests whether CNN models of soil mid-infrared (MIR) spectra, trained on the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), transfer to other spectrometers. It uses the ring trial of Safanelli et al. (2023), in which 20 laboratories scanned the same 70 soils, each with its own instrument and procedure. A Shimadzu instrument in Japan (Hokudai) also scanned 59 of the soils. The targets are organic carbon, clay, pH and exchangeable potassium (Kex).
The ring trial keeps the soils fixed and changes only the instrument. 60 of the soils come from KSSL, the largest part of OSSL. One of the instruments, the IAEA Thermo Nicolet, also measured the Fukushima soils of ossl-fuku-transfer. There the OSSL Kex model failed on the Fukushima spectra, and it is not settled whether the instrument or the soils caused it. If the model works on the IAEA spectra of these soils, the instrument is not the main cause.
The audience is soil scientists who transfer spectral models between instruments, and the readers of ossl-fuku-transfer.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
Design

Data: soilspecdata’s load_ringtrial returns one Spectra per instrument, with the wet chemistry of the 70 soils.
Pretraining: OSSL v1.2 without 38 KSSL samples that are ring-trial soils. Their OSSL spectra correlate with the KSSL instrument’s ring-trial spectra at 0.99999 or more, and their clay, pH and Kex values are identical. The remaining 22 KSSL soils and the 10 NAPT soils have no match in OSSL.
Model: soilspecdl’s default SpectralCNN, the same CNN as in ossl-fuku-transfer, so the results of the two projects compare directly.
Split: on each instrument, grouped k-fold cross-validation over all 70 soils, repeated with different fold assignments. Near-duplicate soils, such as RT_04, RT_05, RT_07, RT_13 and RT_15, stay in one fold. The paper’s Kennard-Stone split (50 calibration and 20 test soils) is not used: it is optimistic, and its test set has only 20 soils.
Scores: Lin’s CCC, the paper’s main metric, and R². Every method uses the same folds, so methods are compared soil by soil, with paired tests.
Experiments, in order:

Zero-shot: the OSSL models on every instrument, against the paper’s Cubist, MBL and PLSR transfer results.
Few-shot: fine-tuning, and a ridge regression on frozen block-4 features, against PLSR trained only on the ring-trial soils of the same instrument, with growing numbers of training soils.
The gains per instrument, against the paper’s instrument clusters and spectral dissimilarity.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
Notebooks

00_data: loads the spectra and the instrument table, groups the near-duplicate soils, and lists the 38 ring-trial soils that are in OSSL.
01_pretrain: trains one CNN each for clay, pH and K on OSSL, without those 38 soils, on SNV spectra, with the training settings of ossl-fuku-transfer but 80 epochs instead of 20.
02_zero_shot: scores the three models on all 21 ring-trial instruments, with no adaptation.
03_instrument_model: models the difference between each instrument and KSSL with a few physical effects shared by all soils, such as a gain, a baseline and a wavenumber shift.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
Set-up
The project uses the soilspec packages (soilspecdl, soilspecdata and soilspectfm) as editable installs from sibling folders:
soilspec/
  ossl-rt-transfer/
  soilspecdl/
  soilspecdata/
  soilspectfm/
Clone the four repositories into one folder, then, in ossl-rt-transfer/:
uv sync --extra dev
The ring-trial data are not public. This repository does not contain them. With access to them, put them in data/ringtrial/ in the workspace folder, beside the project folders. nbdev-test skips the cells that read them. Run nbdev-test --flags rtdata to include them.

title: Pretraining on OSSL
text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from fastcore.test import *
from soilspecdata.datasets.ossl import load_ossl
The cells that read OSSL are marked #| rtdata, like the ring-trial cells of 00_data, and nbdev-test skips them unless you run nbdev-test --flags rtdata. The outputs on this page come from a local run on an Apple silicon GPU (MPS).

Training data

title: Pretraining on OSSL
text:
Preprocessing



preprocess
def preprocess()->soilspectfm.preprocessing.SNV: # Unfitted transform
SNV of each spectrum, the only preprocessing


SNV works on each spectrum separately, so fitting it on OSSL learns nothing that would differ for a ring-trial instrument. There is no derivative filter: the first convolutions of the CNN can learn derivative-like filters if they help.

Pretraining

Load the weights that pretrain saved under fname





pretrain

    X, # Preprocessed OSSL spectra, on `rt_wns`

    fname, # File name for the weights, without extension
    seed:int=42, # Seed for the validation split and the training

Train a SpectralCNN on OSSL, or load the weights that an earlier run saved under fname





model_dir

title: Instrument model
text:
from fastcore.test import *
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
from soilspecdata.datasets.ringtrial import load_ringtrial
from ossl_rt_transfer.data import rt_path, load_instruments, near_dup_groups
The cells that read the ring-trial data are marked #| rtdata. The outputs on this page come from a local run.

title: Instrument model
text:
The model
For each soil, the KSSL spectrum is the reference. The model turns it into the spectrum that another instrument records for the same soil, with parameters shared by all soils of that instrument. The effects, applied in this order to raw absorbance:

shift: a wavenumber shift and stretch, applied by linear interpolation.
broaden: a Gaussian filter, for a coarser resolution.
contrast: absorbance raised to a power γ.
gain: multiplication by a smooth curve.
baseline: addition of a smooth curve.

Gain and baseline are B-splines with 10 basis functions over the whole range.



bspline_basis
def bspline_basis(
    x, # Points to evaluate the basis on, increasing
    n_basis:int=10, # Number of basis functions
    k:int=3, # Degree
)->numpy.ndarray: # One row per point, one column per basis function
Clamped B-spline basis with knots evenly spaced over x



test_close(bspline_basis(np.linspace(0, 1, 50)).sum(1), np.ones(50))




InstrumentModel
def InstrumentModel(
    wn, # Wavenumbers, evenly spaced
    effects:tuple=('gain', 'baseline'), # Any of 'shift', 'broaden', 'contrast', 'gain' and 'baseline'
    n_basis:int=10, # Number of B-spline basis functions for gain and baseline
    max_hw:int=20, # Half-width of the broadening filter, in points
):
Turn reference spectra into the spectra of another instrument, with the effects in effects





snv_t
def snv_t(
    x, # Spectra, one per row
):
SNV of each row of a tensor



wn = np.arange(650, 4001, 2.)
x = torch.rand(3, len(wn), dtype=torch.float64) + 0.5
m = InstrumentModel(wn, ('shift', 'broaden', 'contrast', 'gain', 'baseline'))
test_eq(m(x).shape, x.shape)
test_close(InstrumentModel(wn, ('shift', 'contrast', 'gain', 'baseline'))(x), x)

With the parameters at their starting values, every effect except the broadening leaves the spectra unchanged.

title: Instrument model
text:
Fitting
fit_instrument fits one model to the paired spectra of an instrument and KSSL. The loss compares the SNV of the modelled spectra with the SNV of the measured ones. SNV removes the offset and scale of each scan, so the model needs no parameters for single soils, and the error is on the scale the CNN sees. The CO₂ band is left out.



residuals
def residuals(
    m, wn, Xr, Xi
)->numpy.ndarray: # One row per soil, without the CO₂ band
SNV of the modelled spectra minus SNV of the measured ones





fit_instrument
def fit_instrument(
    wn, # Wavenumbers
    Xr, # Reference spectra
    Xi, # Spectra of the instrument, for the same soils
    effects, # Effects of `InstrumentModel`
    iters:int=300, # Iterations of L-BFGS
)->__main__.InstrumentModel:
Fit an InstrumentModel that turns Xr into Xi, on SNV spectra without the CO₂ band





paired_spectra
def paired_spectra(
    rt, # Ring trial, from `load_ringtrial`
    inst, # Instrument
    ref:str='KSSL', # Reference instrument
)->tuple: # Sample ids, spectra of `inst`, spectra of `ref`, in the same order
Spectra of inst and ref for the soils that both measured



xi = InstrumentModel(wn, ('gain', 'baseline'))
with torch.no_grad(): xi.g.mul_(1.3); xi.b.add_(0.2); y = xi(x)
m = fit_instrument(wn, x.numpy(), y.numpy(), ('gain', 'baseline'))
assert np.abs(residuals(m, wn, x.numpy(), y.numpy())).max() < 1e-4

A model fitted to spectra made with a known gain and baseline reproduces them.

title: Instrument model
text:
Instruments
MSU has the same hardware as KSSL: a Bruker Vertex 70 with the HTS-XT accessory, an MCT detector and a KBr beamsplitter, at 4 cm⁻¹, with pressed samples. What differs is mostly the laboratory. title: Instrument model
text:
Shared and soil-specific differences
Each model adds effects to the one above it. total is the RMS of the SNV residuals. shared is the RMS of their mean over soils: the part a model with shared parameters can remove. soil_specific is what remains after the mean is removed. For comparison, the spread between soils of the KSSL SNV spectra is 0.26.

models = {'none': (), 'gain+baseline': ('gain', 'baseline'), '+shift': ('gain', 'baseline', 'shift'),
          '+broaden': ('gain', 'baseline', 'shift', 'broaden'), '+contrast': ('gain', 'baseline', 'shift', 'broaden', 'contrast')}
def decompose(inst):
    ids, Xi, Xr = paired_spectra(rt, inst); rows = {}
    for name, eff in models.items():
        m = fit_instrument(wn, Xr, Xi, eff); r = residuals(m, wn, Xr, Xi); sh = r.mean(0)
        rows[name] = {'total': np.sqrt((r**2).mean()), 'shared': np.sqrt((sh**2).mean()),
                      'soil_specific': np.sqrt(((r-sh)**2).mean()), **m.params()}
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T
dec = pd.concat({i: decompose(i) for i in insts})

title: Instrument model
text:
Soils left out
The same models, fitted on 4 of 5 folds of soils and scored on the fifth. The folds keep the near-duplicate groups of 00_data together:

groups = pd.Series(near_dup_groups(rt['KSSL']), index=rt['KSSL'].sample_ids)
def cv_rmse(inst, eff, n_splits=5):
    ids, Xi, Xr = paired_spectra(rt, inst); sq = 0.
    for tr, te in GroupKFold(n_splits).split(Xr, groups=groups.loc[ids].values):
        sq += (residuals(fit_instrument(wn, Xr[tr], Xi[tr], eff), wn, Xr[te], Xi[te])**2).mean()*len(te)
    return np.sqrt(sq/len(ids))

title: Instrument model
text:
The soil-specific part
A PCA of the residuals of the full model, after removing their mean. explained is the share of variance of each component. The table also gives the wavenumber of the largest loading, the share of the loading’s energy in the 20 lowest Fourier frequencies, and the correlation of the scores with the soil properties:

src = rt['KSSL'].source
wm = wn[(wn < co2_region[0]) | (wn > co2_region[1])]
def residual_pca(inst, n=3):
    ids, Xi, Xr = paired_spectra(rt, inst)
    r = residuals(fit_instrument(wn, Xr, Xi, models['+contrast']), wn, Xr, Xi); r = r - r.mean(0)
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(r, full_matrices=False)
    props = src.loc[ids, ['clay_perc', 'carbon_org_perc', 'potassium_cmolkg', 'pH_H20']].astype(float)
    rows = []
    for j in range(n):
        f = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(Vt[j]))**2
        sc = pd.Series(U[:, j]*S[j], index=ids)
        rows.append({'explained': S[j]**2/(S**2).sum(), 'peak_cm': wm[np.abs(Vt[j]).argmax()], 'low_freq': f[:20].sum()/f.sum(),
                     **{p: sc.corr(props[p]) for p in props}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, index=[f'pc{j+1}' for j in range(n)])

Three components explain most of the soil-specific part, so it is structured, not noise. The components are smooth, with almost all their energy at low frequencies, and correlate weakly with the soil properties. On MSU, the first lies around 3400 cm⁻¹, the O-H band of water, and the second around 1100 cm⁻¹. On IAEA, the first lies around 1020 cm⁻¹. Both regions are near the Si-O band of quartz and silicates, which in diffuse reflectance depends on particle size and packing. A possible reading is that the soil-specific part comes from how each laboratory prepared and presented each sample, such as moisture and packing, and not from the instrument. This is not tested yet.

title: Instrument model
text:
Naming the components
Two checks on whether the soil-specific components are preparation effects. The residuals of the full model, minus each instrument’s mean, are pooled over the 20 instruments, and one PCA is fitted to them. Each lab’s mean score is then 0, so the table gives each lab’s spread of scores, and the correlation of its scores with clay:

others = [k for k in rt if k != 'KSSL']
R, lab, soil = [], [], []
for k in others:
    ids, Xi, Xr = paired_spectra(rt, k)
    r = residuals(fit_instrument(wn, Xr, Xi, models['+contrast']), wn, Xr, Xi)
    R.append(r - r.mean(0)); lab += [k]*len(ids); soil += list(ids)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(np.vstack(R), full_matrices=False)
Vt = Vt * np.sign(Vt[:, [np.abs(wm-3400).argmin()]]) # Each loading positive at 3400 cm⁻¹
print('explained:', (S[:4]**2/(S**2).sum()).round(3))
for j in range(3):
    pk, _ = find_peaks(np.abs(Vt[j]), distance=15); pk = np.sort(pk[np.argsort(-np.abs(Vt[j][pk]))][:6])
    print(f'pc{j+1} largest loadings:', [(int(wm[p]), round(float(Vt[j][p]), 3)) for p in pk])

The first component lies on the main quartz bands, at 1044-1100, 800 and 694 cm⁻¹. In diffuse reflectance these bands change with particle size. In most labs its scores correlate negatively with clay, so sandier soils, richer in quartz, differ more, as a difference in grinding or packing would make them. UWisc, the only lab with a front-facing accessory, has the opposite sign. The second component is a broad band at 3400-3526 cm⁻¹, with a small rise at 1630 cm⁻¹, as adsorbed water would give. Its scores correlate positively with clay in most labs, and clay soils hold more hygroscopic water. The spread of the first component is smallest for the labs with the HTS-XT accessory of KSSL, and largest for IAEA, UWisc and Lesotho. Lesotho also has a third component far larger than any other lab’s. Presentation, pressed or levelled, makes little difference, and it is confounded with the accessory.

from fastcore.test import *
from soilspecdata.datasets.ringtrial import load_ringtrial
from ossl_rt_transfer.data import rt_path, load_instruments, ossl_props

title: Zero-shot transfer
text:
Scoring



zero_shot
def zero_shot(
    model, # Pretrained model, such as from `load_pretrained`
    spectra, # `Spectra` of one ring-trial instrument, on `rt_wns`
    prop, # Ring-trial property, a key of `ossl_props`
)->dict: # Number of soils, and `regression_scores`
Score model on the soils of one instrument that have a value of prop, with no adaptation to the instrument


zero_shot preprocesses the spectra as in pretraining, and scores the predictions against the measured values. For K, R², r and CCC are on log1p(K), as in pretraining, and RMSE and bias are in cmolc/kg. The 38 ring-trial soils that are in OSSL were left out of pretraining, so every soil is a test soil.

rtd = load_ringtrial(rt_path())
models = {p: load_pretrained(f'ossl_{p}_snv_ep80') for p in ossl_props}
zs = pd.DataFrame([{'instrument': k, 'property': p, **zero_shot(models[p], s, p)} for k, s in rtd.items() for p in ossl_props])
test_eq(len(zs), 21 * 3)
clusters = load_instruments().cluster.reindex(list(rtd)).astype('Int64')
by_inst = lambda col: zs.pivot(index='instrument', columns='property', values=col).assign(cluster=clusters).sort_values(['cluster', 'pH_H20'])
